title: Enlightenment
author: Zhanran (commentary)
excerpt: Enlightenment has two levels: understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. The awakening of sudden enlightenment followed by gradual practice (seeing one's nature) is understanding-awakening; the awakening of gradual practice followed by sudden enlightenment (illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature) is realization-awakening. Sudden enlightenment with gradual practice and gradual practice with sudden enlightenment are two paths of cultivation, each with its own merits.

inline.s: Enlightenment has two levels: understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. The awakening of sudden enlightenment followed by gradual practice (seeing one's nature) is understanding-awakening; the awakening of gradual practice followed by sudden enlightenment (illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature) is realization-awakening. Sudden enlightenment with gradual practice, and gradual practice with sudden enlightenment, are two paths of cultivation, each with its own merits.
[Seeing one's nature] To glimpse one's self-nature and find the master within.
For example, the direct pointing to see one's nature in the Chan koans. [Illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature] To see one's original nature thoroughly (for details, see
Illuminating the Mind and Seeing One's Nature
). As for self-nature and original nature, see
The Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
for details.
Those of sudden enlightenment with gradual practice:
as the Xiuxin Jue says (for details, see
An In-Depth Explanation of the Xiuxin Jue

), first one sees one's nature (awakening), then, relying on this awakening, one begins to practice, doing the work of safeguarding and sustaining (the practice of herding the ox): regulating the mind, eliminating habits, and maintaining samādhi and prajñā in equal measure.
Herding the ox
] To tame the ox of the mind. For details, see
Dahui's Chan Methods
, the chapter on “herding the ox.”
As for the koan of directly pointing to see one's nature, the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp says:

“Chan Master Lingxun of Mount Furong in Fuzhou first went to study under Guizong. He asked, ‘What is the Buddha?’ Guizong said, ‘If I tell you, will you believe it?’ The master said, ‘You speak sincere and truthful words, sir — how dare I not believe?’ Guizong said, ‘This very you is it.’ The master asked, ‘How shall I safeguard and sustain it?’ Guizong said, ‘With a single film over the eye, flowers fall in confusion from the empty sky.’”

[Safeguard and sustain] To protect and let things take their natural course. [With a single film over the eye, flowers fall in confusion from the empty sky] One with an eye ailment sees flowers (blossoms) in the sky, though in truth there are none. The meaning of “with a single film over the eye, flowers fall in confusion from the empty sky” is: do not let delusion veil the original mind.

In this koan, Chan Master Lingxun suddenly heard “this very you is it (you are the Buddha),” and was jolted! At the instant his stream of thought was cut off, he glimpsed his self-nature and found the master within (sudden enlightenment). He then asked how to safeguard and sustain it (gradual practice).
Those of gradual practice with sudden enlightenment:
taking enlightenment as the goal, investigating to the very end until one thoroughly sees one's original nature (illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature). The Venerable Xuyun said:
“investigate a single huatou until enlightenment
(illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature)
as the goal.”
(from the Venerable Xuyun's Expedient Instructions)

The enlightenment spoken of here is the shedding of sense-faculties and sense-objects and the thorough seeing of one's original nature. As recorded in the Wudeng Huiyuan, Chan Master Baizhang ascended the hall and said:

“The spiritual light shines alone, far transcending the senses and their objects. The essence is revealed in its true eternity, not bound by words and letters. The mind's nature is undefiled, originally perfect and complete. Only let go of delusive conditions
(only do not deludedly cling to sense-objects),
and you are the Buddha of thusness.”
As for understanding-awakening and realization-awakening, Master Hanshan instructed in his Collection of Dream Wanderings, “Reply to Governor Zheng Kunyan”:

[Among practitioners, some awaken first and cultivate afterward, and some cultivate first and awaken afterward; yet awakening differs between understanding and realization. One who illuminates the mind by relying on the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs has understanding-awakening; such a one mostly falls into intellectual views, and in all situations and circumstances is mostly without power. Because mind and objects stand opposed and cannot merge, at every turn there is obstruction and many hindrances. This is called semblance-prajñā, and is not genuine investigation.]

Among practitioners, some awaken first and cultivate afterward (sudden enlightenment with gradual practice), and some cultivate first and awaken afterward (gradual practice with sudden enlightenment); hence awakening divides into understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. One who illuminates the mind by relying on the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs (this is seeing one's nature) has understanding-awakening. Those with understanding-awakening mostly fall into intellectual views, and in all situations and circumstances are mostly without power. This is because mind and objects are still in a state of opposition and have not yet merged; thus, on meeting objects and encountering conditions, one is at once entangled, with many hindrances. This is semblance-prajñā, not genuine investigation.

[But one with realization-awakening, from within one's own mind, works on plainly and honestly, pressing onward until the water is exhausted and the mountains end; suddenly a single thought comes to rest, and one thoroughly understands one's own mind — like meeting one's own father at a crossroads, with nothing further to doubt. It is like a person drinking water, who alone knows whether it is warm or cold, and cannot disclose it to others. This is genuine investigation and true awakening. Thereafter, using the point of awakening, one merges mind and objects, purifies the manifest karmic stream of consciousness, and melts deluded thoughts and emotional concerns into a single-flavored true mind. This is realization-awakening.]

But one with realization-awakening works down solidly and honestly from within one's own mind (whether the work of observing the mind or the work of investigating Chan), pressing onward until the water is exhausted and the mountains end; suddenly a single thought (a subtle thought) comes to rest, and one thoroughly awakens to one's own mind (this is illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature) — like meeting one's own father at a crossroads and recognizing him at a glance, without doubting whether it is he. This state, like a person drinking water, its warmth or coldness only oneself knows, and one cannot tell it to others. This is genuine investigation and true awakening. Thereafter, using the point of awakening, one merges mind and objects, purifies the manifest karmic stream of consciousness, and melts deluded thoughts and emotional concerns entirely into a single-flavored true mind. This is realization-awakening.
In the Jideng Lu (Continuation of the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), Chan Master Mengshan Deyi relates in his own words the course of his investigating Chan and awakening:
I
(Chan Master Mengshan Deyi referring to himself)
at the age of twenty, knew of this matter
(illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature).

By thirty-two, I had consulted seventeen or eighteen elder monks, asking them how to do the work, and none of them had a definitive answer. Later I studied under the elder Wanshan, who taught me to look into the word ‘wu’ (no). Through all twelve periods of the day I was to remain alert, like a cat catching a mouse, like a hen brooding over her eggs, never allowing an interruption. Before breaking through, I was like a mouse gnawing at a coffin
(only by gnawing through can it stay alive),
unable to change my course. Working in this way, there would surely come a time of
(the sudden blooming of the mind's flower)
illumination. So day and night I diligently
(untiringly)
investigated. After eighteen days, while
(drinking tea),
I suddenly understood ‘the World-Honored One held up a flower, and Kāśyapa smiled,’ and was overjoyed beyond measure.
(“Suddenly understood” — this is understanding-awakening.)

I sought confirmation from three or four elder monks, but none said a word. One taught me simply to seal it fast with the ocean-seal samādhi and pay no heed to anything else, and I believed this instruction.

[Ocean-seal samādhi] When delusions cease and the mind is clear, the myriad forms appear at once, like the surface of a calm, clear sea that reflects every image. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “When I press my finger, the ocean-seal radiates light; the moment you stir your mind, the dust of affliction arises first.”
After two years
(after two years),
in the fifth year of Jingding
(the fifth year of Jingding in the Southern Song, the year
in the sixth month, in the prefecture of Chongqing in Sichuan, I fell ill with dysentery
(contracted dysentery),
a hundred times by day and night
(a hundred bouts of diarrhea by day and night).
Critically ill and near death, I was entirely without power
(my work was entirely without power).

The ocean-seal samādhi was of no use; my former understanding was of no use. My mouth could not speak, my body could not move; there was nothing but death. Karmic circumstances and states all appeared at once
(I experienced firsthand that understanding-awakening cannot withstand birth and death),

and I was stricken with terror and panic, beset by many sufferings at once. So I forced myself to take charge, gave instructions for my final affairs, set the meditation cushion high, prepared a censer of incense, slowly sat up in meditation, and silently prayed to the Three Jewels and the dragons and devas, repenting of all my past unwholesome karma: if my life's end should come, may I, sustained by the power of prajñā, be reborn with right mindfulness and leave home early; if I should recover from this illness, may I renounce the lay life and become a monk, soon attain awakening, and widely deliver later students.

Having made this vow, I took up the word ‘wu’ and turned the light back to look at myself. Before long, my internal organs stirred three or four times, but I paid them no heed. After a long while, my eyelids ceased to move. After another long while, I no longer perceived my body; only the huatou continued without ceasing. It was evening before I rose, and my illness had receded by half. I sat again until the fourth point of the third watch of the night, and all my illnesses had receded completely; body and mind were light and at ease.
In the eighth month I went to Jiangling and had my head shaved
(took the tonsure to become a monk),
and a year later I set out
(left the monastery)

on pilgrimage. While cooking rice on the road, I realized that the work must be done in one continuous stretch and must not be interrupted. When I arrived at Huanglong and entered the hall, the first time the sleep-demon came I roused my spirits on the seat and lightly repelled it. The second time I repelled it the same way. The third time, when the sleep-demon was heavy, I got down and made prostrations to dispel it, then returned to the cushion. With this regimen fixed, I seized the moment to do battle with
(to gather up and settle)

the sleep-demon. At first I slept briefly on a pillow, then on my arm, and finally did not lie down at all. After two or three nights I was weary day and night, and my steps felt light and floating. Suddenly, before my eyes it was as though dark clouds parted, and my body felt as clean and refreshed as one newly bathed coming out of the water. The mass of doubt in my mind grew ever stronger; without applying force, it presented itself continuously. All forms and sounds, the five desires and the eight winds, could not enter. I was as pure as a silver basin filled with snow, as solemn as the clear air of autumn.

[The five desires] Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means pleasing and melodious sounds; fragrance means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means agreeable tactile pleasure. Because these five can give rise to a mind of greed, they are called the five desires. [The eight winds] Gain and loss, slander and praise, honor and blame, suffering and joy.
Then I reflected that, though the work was good, there was no one to resolve my doubts
(no good teacher to decide my doubts and discern the principle),
so I left the monastery
(and set out to visit other teachers),

entering Zhejiang. The hardships of the road caused my work to regress. Arriving at the place of the Venerable Guchan of Chengtian and joining the hall there, I vowed: until I attained awakening, I would never leave
(would never leave this monastery).
After a month or so, my work was restored
(the work was restored).
At that time sores broke out all over my body, but I paid them no heed, pursuing the matter with my life
(investigating),
and my work naturally gained power; I could even do the work while ill.
Because I went out the gate to attend a vegetarian feast, I walked along holding the huatou, and without realizing it walked past the host's house — and so I could also do the work while moving.
By now
(by this time, the mass of doubt)
was like moonlight piercing the water: on a rushing rapid, amid turbulent waves, it could not be scattered by contact or lost by tossing, but remained vividly alive.
On the sixth day of the third month, as I sat holding up the word ‘wu,’ the head monk entered the hall to burn incense, and the striking of the incense box made a sound. Suddenly,
crash!
with that sound, I recognized myself
(recognized my own original face — this is realization-awakening),
and caught Zhaozhou at last
(penetrated Zhaozhou's ‘wu’ koan).
Then I composed a verse: Luckless
(hapless),
at the road's end, kicking over the wave, it is water
(awakening to the fact that the wave is water);
the peerless old Zhaozhou,
(the outstanding old Venerable Zhaozhou),
his face is only thus
(his original face is no different from what I have awakened to).
[Moonlight] The brightness of the moon. [Bobo,
bō bō
] a lively, vivid appearance.
In autumn, at Lin'an, I saw the great elders Xueyan, Tuigeng, Shikeng, and Xuzhou. Xuzhou urged me to go to Wanshan. Wanshan
(that is, Chan Master Wanshan Yugu Xian)

asked, ‘Bright light silently shining everywhere, pervading the Ganges' sands — is this not the words of the scholar Zhang Zhuo?’ The moment I opened my mouth, Wanshan shouted me out. From then on, whether walking, sitting, or eating, everything seemed meaningless. After six months, in the spring of the following year, returning from outside the city, as I climbed the stone steps, suddenly the obstruction of doubt in my breast melted like ice, and I was no longer aware of my body walking on the road. Then I saw Wanshan, and Wanshan asked the same words again; I at once overturned the meditation seat. And the several extremely perplexing koans from before I understood one by one.
[Bright light silently shining everywhere, pervading the Ganges' sands — is this not the words of the scholar Zhang Zhuo]
This was Chan Master Wanshan Yugu Xian having him investigate Zhang Zhuo's verse, to make both existence and nonexistence disappear for him.
The Wudeng Huiyuan records:
The scholar Zhang Zhuo, at the direction of Master Chanyue, went to study under Shishuang
(the scholar Zhang Zhuo, following Master Chanyue's guidance, went to visit Chan Master Shishuang).

Shishuang asked, “What is your surname, scholar?” He said, “My surname is Zhang and my name is Zhuo (Clumsy).” Shishuang said, “Even seeking cleverness you cannot obtain it — from where would clumsiness come?”

(Even cleverness cannot be sought and obtained, so where is there any clumsiness? This is Chan Master Shishuang speaking of the true reality of all dharmas through Zhang Zhuo's name, guiding him into the gate of non-duality.)
Zhang Zhuo
(Zhang Zhuo)
suddenly had an awakening
(a sudden great awakening),
and presented this verse, saying:
Bright light, in stillness shining, fills the Ganges' sands; / both sage and common — all that live — share with me this home.
When not a single thought arises, the whole body stands revealed; / the moment the six senses stir, by clouds it is concealed.
To cut away affliction only adds disease anew; / to strive toward suchness is itself a devious view.
Follow worldly conditions without hindrance or regret — / nirvāṇa and birth-and-death are flowers in empty air as yet.
This verse is Zhang Zhuo's description of his own state after his great awakening, presented to Chan Master Shishuang for confirmation. The verse is explained as follows:
[Bright light, in stillness shining, fills the Ganges' sands]

This describes the state of thoroughly seeing one's original nature at awakening: the original nature is bright, clear, and still, shining everywhere over worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
[The ordinary and the holy, all sentient beings, share this home with me]

The self-nature of ordinary beings and sages is the same as that which is in my home (my self-nature). “Containing spirit” means that which possesses spirituality, referring to sentient beings; but in this line it refers to self-nature. This line says that the self-nature of ordinary beings and sages is the same as my self-nature: those whose self-nature is deluded are ordinary beings, and those whose self-nature is awakened are sages.
[When not a single thought arises, the whole body stands revealed]
When not a single thought arises (coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and the subtlest thoughts all cease), then the original nature is thoroughly revealed (the whole body appears).
[The moment the six senses stir, by clouds it is concealed]
The moment the six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) stir, the inherent light of self-nature is at once veiled by afflictions and assumes the state of habitual tendencies.
[To cut away affliction only adds disease anew]

Self-nature is luminous and clear, still and silent, complete with all virtues, and perfect from the very beginning. To stir the mind and thoughts to cut away afflictions only adds to delusion. The Xiuxin Jue says:

“Not knowing that good and evil are empty by nature, sitting rigidly without moving, pressing down the body and mind like a stone pressing down grass, and taking this for cultivating the mind — this is a great delusion! Hence it is said: ‘The śrāvaka cuts off delusion with thought after thought’
(the delusions of views and thoughts),

‘yet the mind that cuts is itself a thief.’ Only observe truly that killing, stealing, lust, and lying arise from the nature; arising is no-arising, and right where they are, they are at once quiescent — why need one cut them further? Hence it is said: ‘Do not fear the arising of thoughts; only fear being slow to awaken.’ And again: ‘When a thought arises, awaken at once; once awakened, it is gone.’ Therefore, for an awakened person, even adventitious defilements all become clarified butter. Only illuminate that delusion has no root: the three realms of sky-flowers are like mist blown away by the wind, and the six illusory dusts are like ice melted by hot water.”

But one should note that after awakening, there are two gates of practice: the gate of letting things be (renyun) and the gate of applying antidotes. “To cut away affliction only adds disease anew” and the next line, “to strive toward suchness is itself a devious view,” speak of the gate of letting things be. If one has awakened but one's foundation is insufficient, one's afflictions are dense, and one's habits are strong and heavy, so that one cannot accomplish “only illuminate that delusion has no root: the three realms of sky-flowers are like mist blown away by the wind, and the six illusory dusts are like ice melted by hot water,” then one should first enter the gate of applying antidotes, and must not deludedly cling to “to cut away affliction only adds disease anew” and thereby “indulge oneself at will.”

[The delusions of views and thoughts] The delusions of views and the delusions of thoughts. The delusions of views are the errors and misconceptions of ordinary beings in their understanding, namely the five false views: the view of a self, the extreme views, false views, the view of clinging to views, and the view of clinging to precepts. The delusions of thoughts are the errors and misconceptions of ordinary beings in their thinking, namely the afflictions of greed, hatred, ignorance, pride, and doubt. These two kinds of delusion are the root of sentient beings' cycle of birth and death; cutting them off ends birth and death and escapes the cycle of rebirth.
[Clarified butter] Milk refined through many processes; first among flavors and first among medicines. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
“Clarified butter is called the foremost and highest flavor in the world.”
And again:
“Among all medicines, clarified butter is first, excellently curing the feverish and agitated minds of sentient beings.”
[To strive toward suchness is itself a devious view]

To stir the mind to head toward suchness (the original nature) is also mistaken, because for self-nature to manifest the state of the original nature, not only must coarse and fine thoughts cease, but even the subtlest thoughts must cease — how can one stir the mind and thoughts to return to the source (to head toward it)?
[Follow worldly conditions without hindrance]

Now that one has thoroughly awakened to the ultimate truth, one follows worldly conditions and, without hindrance, transforms and lives out one's days: when conditions come, one responds; when conditions go, one rests in stillness.
[The ultimate truth] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth, namely the true reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are false and empty; where they cease, that is called the real, is called true reality, is called the dharmadhātu, is called ultimate wisdom, is called the ultimate truth, is called the ultimate emptiness.”
(from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra)
[Nirvāṇa and birth-and-death are alike empty flowers]
Because nirvāṇa and birth-and-death are both illusions (empty flowers). The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like last night's dream.”

All you benevolent ones, in investigating Chan you must be very careful. If I had not fallen gravely ill in Chongqing, I would have almost passed my life in vain. What matters most is to meet a person of right knowledge and right views. That is why the ancients visited teachers in the morning and sought instruction in the evening, examining body and mind with diligence and earnestness, to clarify this matter.”

[If I had not fallen gravely ill in Chongqing, I would have almost passed my life in vain] Had I not fallen gravely ill in Chongqing, near death, and experienced it firsthand, I would not have known that understanding-awakening cannot
withstand

birth and death, and I would have almost passed my whole life in vain. This firsthand experience — that understanding-awakening cannot withstand birth and death — was also had in his youth by Chan Master Yuanwu Keqin, the teacher of Dahui; it is a warning bell for practitioners.
The Sengbao Zhengxu Zhuan records:
Chan Master Keqin took refuge under Wuzu Fayan: “The master
(Keqin)
relied on his eloquent argument and contended sharply with him. Fayan was displeased
(Fayan was displeased; yì means to be pleased),
and said, ‘Can this withstand birth and death
(can your eloquence withstand birth and death)?
Another day, when the lamp burns alone in the nirvāṇa hall, test it for yourself!’
(Keqin)
left because of this disagreement. Arriving at Dinghui in Suzhou, he fell gravely ill and nearly died. He then recalled his former
(past)
investigations, all without effect
(at the point of death, all his former work of investigation was of no effect, and at the juncture of birth and death he could not be master),
and only old Fayan had not deceived me
(only the old teacher Fayan did not deceive me, speaking the truth to me: ‘Can this withstand birth and death?’)
As soon as he recovered from his illness, he packed up that very day and returned
(the moment he was well, he gathered his belongings that day and went back to Fayan).
Fayan rejoiced at his return and accepted him as an attendant.
[Wuzu Fayan] In his later years Chan Master Fayan lived at Dongchan Monastery on Mount Wuzu in Qizhou, and was known in the world as “Wuzu Fayan” (Fayan of the Fifth Patriarch).
